entries.clue: Zero choice, quietly moving to find romantic elixir (4,6)

indicatorNotes.moving: Something moving does not stay where it was put, so the letter named beside it takes up a different place in its word.

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis scoring
an option is a choice, and p is the musical mark for quietly; that p shifts to the front of the six letters
the instruction that sends the p forward

annotation.surface: Left with no choice, somebody slips away quietly in search of a love drug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' is not adding a letter here — the p is already sitting in the choice, and the clue is telling you where it goes instead. Love for zero comes from the tennis court.
annotation.definitionFit: An elixir is a magic drink, and a love potion is the one in folklore that makes whoever swallows it fall for the giver.

entries.clue: Primarily, location inviting dipping outdoors? (4)

indicatorNotes.Primarily: Primarily means first of all, so each word that follows hands over the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the four words, taken in order

annotation.surface: A place, first and foremost, that invites you to take a dip in the open air.
annotation.walkthrough: A lido is a British open-air public swimming pool, most of them built between the wars. Every word is doing two jobs at once: describing the thing and surrendering its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a lido is a location that invites dipping outdoors, which is what an open-air pool is for.

entries.clue: Meteorological device useless in broadcast (4)

indicatorNotes.in broadcast: Anything broadcast is heard rather than read, so it is the sound of the word that matters and not its spelling.

blocks.note: vain means useless, as in a vain attempt, and the two spellings come out of the mouth identically

annotation.surface: A weather instrument written off as useless on the forecast.
annotation.walkthrough: A weather vane is the arrow on a church spire that swings round to show the wind direction. Vain, vane and vein are a standard crossword trio, and only the context tells you which is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: A vane is the pivoting arrow that shows which way the wind is blowing, which makes it a device for reading the weather.

entries.clue: Before jobs advertised, terms often stated? (12)

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before, as in pre-war
positions is the word job advertisements use for the jobs on offer

annotation.surface: A job advertisement setting out the terms on offer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Before' is itself one of the words the answer names, so the clue opens with a specimen of its own solution. 'Terms' is grammar's word for a class of word, and these are the ones English says most.
annotation.definitionFit: Prepositions — of, to, in, for — are the grammatical terms that come out of an English speaker's mouth more often than any other words.

entries.clue: Sweet time raising tiny creature with expensive coat (7)

indicatorNotes.raising: To raise something in a down clue is to lift it up the grid, so the letters that follow are written upwards, which is backwards.

blocks.note: t = time, the standard abbreviation
an elf is the small creature of folklore
fur is the costly coat, the animal's and the garment's alike
reversal indicator: the two pieces go in upwards

annotation.surface: A pleasant spell spent bringing up a small animal that wears an expensive coat.
annotation.walkthrough: Only a down clue can use 'raising', which lifts letters up the page and so writes them backwards. A truffle is also the fungus that pigs root out of the soil, and that one is the expensive item.
annotation.definitionFit: A truffle is the small round chocolate, so 'sweet' is the British noun for a piece of confectionery rather than the taste.

entries.clue: In Oxford English Dictionary, slang for 'hand' left out (7)

indicatorNotes.In: In puts one thing inside another, so the letters named after the comma go within the letters named first.

blocks.note: the Oxford English Dictionary is known by its initials
a mitt is slang for a hand

annotation.surface: A slang word for hand that never made it into the dictionary.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has the slang missing from the dictionary; the wordplay does the opposite and shuts it inside. Mitt comes from boxing — get your mitts off — which is how it came to stand for a hand.
annotation.definitionFit: To omit something is to leave it out, whether it is a name missing from a list or a verse dropped from a hymn.

entries.clue: Without partisanship? Not entirely ... (4)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: Not entirely means you are not to use the whole word, so what is wanted is a run of the letters inside it.

blocks.note: four letters running unbroken through the middle of the word

annotation.surface: Someone admitting they are not entirely free of party bias.
annotation.walkthrough: Sans is French for without, kept alive in English by 'sans serif' and by Shakespeare's 'sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything'. Most hidden answers straddle two words; this one sits inside a single long one.
annotation.definitionFit: Sans means without — the French preposition, borrowed whole into English and still used where a touch of style is wanted.

entries.clue: Fond of food, topless, enormous (10)

indicatorNotes.topless: Topless takes the top off, and the top of a word written down the grid is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: gastronomic means devoted to good eating
the g at the top comes away

annotation.surface: A huge shirtless man who is fond of his food.
annotation.walkthrough: Astronomic reaches 'enormous' by way of distance rather than bulk — the scale of the stars. Three plain adjectives in a row give no sign that the middle one is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Astronomic figures are the ones too big to picture, the word having drifted from the stars to any enormous quantity.

entries.clue: Customer for whom every purchase is a steal? (10)

annotation.definition: Customer for whom every purchase is a steal?

blocks.note: 'a steal' is what a shopper calls a bargain, so the surface is somebody delighted with the prices
the generous word: this one walks out of the shop without paying for anything

annotation.surface: A bargain hunter thrilled with the prices in the local shop.
annotation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here — no indicator, no fodder, no letters to move — so the clue is one sentence with two readings, and the question mark is the warning. 'A steal' does the pivoting.
annotation.definitionFit: A shoplifter takes the goods without paying, so every purchase really is stolen, while the shopper's 'a steal' means nothing worse than a bargain.

entries.clue: DJ's tunes displaying acumen: disco, mostly (5,5)

indicatorNotes.displaying: To display something is to lay it out for people to look at, and letters laid out afresh come in a fresh order.
indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly means most of the word and not all of it, so the final letter is left off.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
disco without its last letter, four more letters of fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A DJ's playlist showing good judgement, mostly disco.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon reads as 'namely', as though the clue were about to list the DJ's tunes; it is really the join between definition and fodder. Disco is a kind of dance music, so seeing the word there is no help at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Dance music is the catch-all for what a DJ plays to keep a floor moving — house, techno, garage and disco alike.

entries.clue: Shakespearean ass stripped off, revealing German lad (4)

indicatorNotes.stripped off: To strip off is to take your outer things away, so the word loses the letters at both of its ends.

blocks.note: Bottom is the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream who is given an ass's head
the outer b and m come away

annotation.surface: Shakespeare's donkey-headed weaver undressing to reveal a German boy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stripped off' does double duty: the ass in question is Bottom, a weaver already transformed out of his own shape. 'German lad' defines by example — Bismarck, Otto the Great — with no question mark to warn you.
annotation.definitionFit: Otto is a common German man's name, from Bismarck to Otto the Great, so the definition names the answer by example.

entries.clue: Another swindle from junior partner (6,6)

blocks.note: another helping is a second one
a fiddle is a swindle — fiddling the books

annotation.surface: The junior partner in a firm has pulled yet another fast one.
annotation.walkthrough: Playing second fiddle means taking the lesser part beside somebody more important; the phrase comes from the orchestra, where the second violins follow the firsts. The clue's junior partner works in an office, the answer's anywhere at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To play second fiddle is to be the junior partner in any pairing, the one who follows rather than leads.

entries.clue: Paper in error, ultimately, with the glib Grease To Lose Steam (2,3,3,4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so each of the words it governs gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: a goof is an error, the sort you make yourself
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink British business daily
the closing letters of with, the and glib
grease and oil are the same slippery stuff

annotation.surface: A newspaper getting its facts wrong about the slick musical Grease.
annotation.walkthrough: Grease is italicised because it is the musical, and the clue wants the substance instead. Three small words in a row surrender only their last letters, which is why 'with the' looks like padding and is not.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that goes off the boil loses its heat and its momentum, the same picture as losing steam but taken from the kitchen rather than the engine.

entries.clue: Uselessly intervened - vis-à-vis wheel? (10)

indicatorNotes.Uselessly: A thing done uselessly is done to no purpose, and letters shoved about to no purpose finish in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody stepping in to no purpose where a wheel is concerned.
annotation.walkthrough: To reinvent the wheel is the standard phrase for redoing work already done, so the clue describes its own answer while also being the letters of it. 'Vis-à-vis' means regarding, and does no mechanical work.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: reinventing the wheel is the proverbial useless intervention, labour spent on something finished long ago.

entries.clue: Inertia - flipping extremes in inertia - then assumes proud position (6,4)

indicatorNotes.flipping: To flip two things is to turn them over so the other comes up, so where one of the pair stood the other now goes.

blocks.note: a standstill is inertia — nothing moving at all
the word inertia begins with i and ends with a; the i gives way to the a

annotation.surface: Somebody mired in inertia who then draws themselves up proudly.
annotation.walkthrough: The word 'inertia' is used twice over, once for what it means and once for the two letters at its ends. A dash on either side makes the middle phrase look like an aside, and it is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand tall is to hold yourself upright and unashamed, which is the proud position the definition asks for.

entries.clue: Topless bloke - given plonk - to start weaving? (7)

indicatorNotes.Topless: A word's top is the letter it starts with, so a topless one begins a letter late.

blocks.note: a gent is a bloke; take the top off and the g goes
plonk is British slang for cheap wine

annotation.surface: A shirtless man handed cheap wine and beginning to lurch about.
annotation.walkthrough: The plonk is doing the surface's work: a man given cheap wine really does start weaving, in the staggering sense, and that is where the clue wants you looking. The answer's weaving is done with strands.
annotation.definitionFit: To entwine is to wind strands around each other, which is where any weaving starts.

entries.clue: Unload - and snooze (4,3)

blocks.note: setting down a passenger or a parcel and leaving it there
the short unplanned sleep that comes over you in an armchair

annotation.surface: Getting the shopping out of the car, then having a nap.
annotation.walkthrough: You drop someone off at the station and you drop off in front of the television — one phrase, two senses, with a dash as the only join between them. Nodding off is the same picture, the head falling forward.
annotation.definitionFit: To drop something off is to deliver or unload it; to drop off is also to fall asleep, the head dropping as you go.

entries.clue: Might one of these have an issue with kids ...? (7)

annotation.definition: Might one of these have an issue with kids ...?

blocks.note: the phrase as a parent would use it: trouble with the children
pointing at a class of farm animal, for whom issue is offspring and kids are the young

annotation.surface: A childminder struggling with the children in her charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is the legal and biblical word for offspring — died without issue — and a kid is a young goat, so a nanny goat has issue with kids in the plainest sense. The ellipsis runs on into 19 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A nanny is a female goat: kids are her young and issue is the old word for offspring, while the same word names the human childminder the surface suggests.

entries.clue: Game licence's not beginning to show discipline (7)

indicatorNotes.Game: Game means up for anything, and letters that are game for anything will go in whatever order you please.
indicatorNotes.not beginning: A word not beginning is one that starts a letter late, its first letter dropped.

blocks.note: licence's without its opening l, the apostrophe not counted
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A hunting licence showing no sign of any discipline.
annotation.walkthrough: A game licence is a real thing — the permit for shooting game — which is why the first two words read as one idea. The apostrophe-s is quietly one of the seven letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A science is a discipline in the academic sense: a body of study with its own methods, like physics or geology.

entries.clue: ... Labour leader? (7)

blocks.note: the party reading the capital L invites: whoever is in charge at Westminster
the ellipsis carries the kids over from the clue before, so labour is the other kind — the hours before a birth

annotation.surface: The politician at the head of the Labour party.
annotation.walkthrough: Labour keeps its capital, which pushes you towards the party and the leadership. A midwife leads a woman through labour of the other sort, and the ellipsis from 17 across has already put kids in your head.
annotation.definitionFit: A midwife takes the lead through labour in the childbirth sense, guiding the mother rather than governing a party.

entries.clue: Taking some paracetamol, do VapoRub somewhere in E Europe (7)

indicatorNotes.Taking some: Taking some of a thing means using a part of it and leaving the rest, so an unbroken run of the letters is wanted.

blocks.note: the letters run on unbroken from the end of the painkiller, through the next word and into the third

annotation.surface: Somebody dosing themselves with painkillers and vapour rub in eastern Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: VapoRub's capital V in the middle of a word is exactly the sort of thing that stops the eye running straight through the letters. Moldova is the small landlocked country between Romania and Ukraine.
annotation.definitionFit: Moldova is a country in eastern Europe, wedged between Romania and Ukraine, so the definition places it rather than offering a synonym.

entries.clue: Aromatherapist's regular purchase, must-have painting (9,3)

blocks.note: a must-have is something you cannot do without
an oil is a painting done in oils

annotation.surface: An aromatherapist's usual shopping, and a painting no collection should be without.
annotation.walkthrough: Oil for a painting is a crossword staple, the medium standing in for the picture. The comma after 'purchase' is the only mark of where the definition stops and the two pieces start.
annotation.definitionFit: Essential oils are the concentrated plant extracts an aromatherapist works with, bought by the small bottle week after week.

entries.clue: 'Terrible bore' largely describing Everyman as a writer (4)

indicatorNotes.Terrible: Terrible describes a thing gone wrong, and letters gone wrong are letters out of their proper order.
indicatorNotes.largely: Largely means the large part of it rather than all, so the word gives up its last letter.
indicatorNotes.describing: To describe a circle around something is to draw round it, so these letters go outside the one named next.

blocks.note: bore drops its final letter and the three that remain are shuffled
the setter signs himself Everyman, so his word for himself is the first person

annotation.surface: Somebody dismissing the setter, in his writing, as a terrible bore.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman means himself whenever his name turns up in a clue, and the crossword's first person is a single letter. A biro is a ballpoint, named after its Hungarian inventor László Bíró.
annotation.definitionFit: A biro is a ballpoint pen, and a pen is 'a writer' in the sense of the thing that does the writing rather than the person holding it.

entries.clue: No more than a lake (4)

blocks.note: the belittling sense: only that, and nothing beyond it
a stretch of standing water, the sense kept alive in northern place names

annotation.surface: Something dismissed as being only a lake.
annotation.walkthrough: A mere is a lake — the word inside Windermere and Grasmere — and it survives in English chiefly in those names. Read straight through, the clue is writing something off as nothing much, which is where the second sense hides.
annotation.definitionFit: Mere means no more than, as in a mere boy, and a mere is also a lake, as in Windermere, so both halves are the same four letters.

entries.clue: Ruse; persona backfired (4)

indicatorNotes.backfired: Something that backfires comes back at you the way it went out, so the letters are read from the far end.

blocks.note: a part is a persona — the role an actor takes on

annotation.surface: An assumed identity that blew up in somebody's face.
annotation.walkthrough: The semicolon does nothing but separate definition from wordplay, which leaves a three-word clue with no cover story at all. 'Backfired' reverses across the grid; a down entry would need a word about going up.
annotation.definitionFit: A trap is a ruse: a trick laid for somebody who does not see it coming.

entries.clue: Gnome, idiot, ridiculously early (2,4,4)

indicatorNotes.ridiculously: Something done ridiculously is done in a way that makes no sense, and letters in no sensible order are letters to be rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A run of insults aimed at somebody who turned up absurdly early.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ridiculously' sits between the fodder and the definition and can be read with either, so the comma in front of it is the only hint of where it belongs. In good time means with time in hand, not merely on time.
annotation.definitionFit: To arrive in good time is to arrive with time to spare, which is what early means when nobody is complaining about it.

entries.clue: Artist, Dutch heavyweight (4)

blocks.note: d = Dutch, the usual shortening for the language
Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion

annotation.surface: A Dutch boxer fighting in the heavyweight division.
annotation.walkthrough: Ali is the crossword's boxer and always the heavyweight. Dalí was Spanish, not Dutch — the nationality belongs to the wordplay and not to the man, and his accent is dropped in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: Salvador Dalí painted the melting clocks and the lobster telephone, so 'artist' defines him by the class he belongs to.

entries.clue: Becoming tongue-twisted, lay eyes on a foe, tentacled beast (3,7)

indicatorNotes.Becoming tongue-twisted: A tongue that twists turns one phrase into another that sounds almost the same, so the answer is heard rather than spelt out.

blocks.note: to lay eyes on somebody is to see them and a foe is an enemy; said at speed the two phrases are barely distinguishable

annotation.surface: Catching sight of an enemy and, apparently, of something with tentacles.
annotation.walkthrough: The join between the words moves when you say it: three words become two, and the m and n swap places in the mouth rather than on the page. A sea anemone is the flower-like polyp clinging to rocks in a pool.
annotation.definitionFit: A sea anemone is an animal despite the flower name, a rock-pool polyp that catches its food with a ring of stinging tentacles.
